passage:
Fifteen weeks before the entrance test, Raghav counted the Sundays on a calendar. He listed every unit in the syllabus, divided them across the weeks, and left room for going over old units and mock papers. Each evening was split into three blocks of an hour and a half; a wall chart got a tick for each one done and a cross for each one missed, and on Sundays the crosses moved to the coming week.

Shreya's corner of the classroom was different. "Only one college," she said when Vishal mentioned a second list. "A backup would jinx it." She kept studying hard, but the results came out short of what the college wanted. She had no applications ready, and the next three weeks went by in tears and phone calls.

Raghav's third mock score dropped. He checked his sleep and found gaps in mechanics. For two weeks he skipped his Saturday cricket, added a small daily set of physics problems, and wrote each mock score in a column to see whether the line climbed again.

qa.q: How many weeks before the entrance test did Raghav count the Sundays?
qa.a: He counted them fifteen weeks before the entrance test.

qa.q: What did Raghav do when his third mock score dropped that Shreya could not do when her results fell short?
qa.a: Raghav checked his sleep and gaps, changed his schedule and tracked the scores, while Shreya had no backup applications ready and lost weeks in panic.

qa.q: What was Shreya probably feeling when the results came out short?
qa.a: Distress and panic: she had no applications ready and the next weeks passed in tears.

qa.q: What could Shreya do next?
qa.a: Shreya could talk with a teacher or family about options and start applying to colleges that fit her results.

grounding: Four approaches to entrance exam preparation: working backward, time-boxed blocks with review, refusing a backup, and adjusting after a bad mock.

passage:
Chinmay opened the screen-time report on a Monday and stared. Six hours a day, mostly short videos. He felt less guilty than curious, and wrote the numbers on a sticky note, deciding to plan from those rather than from shame.

Bidisha asked herself a different question: why do I scroll at night? Honest answers came slowly. She felt lonely once her room went quiet, and the unfinished homework worried her. So she wrote two replacements: call a friend for ten minutes, and begin homework with tiny goals of ten minutes each.

Mridul announced in the class group, "No screens for a month, starting today!" But the school groups ran on messages, and homework updates were in there. On day four Mridul opened the chat, felt like a failure, and deleted the whole plan.

Weeks later Chinmay binged all weekend. Instead of quitting, he asked what set it off: a quarrel with his cousin and a long, empty afternoon. He planned a cycling outing for the next Saturday and started again on Monday.

qa.q: How many hours a day did the report show for Chinmay?
qa.a: It showed six hours a day, mostly short videos.

qa.q: How did Bidisha's approach to night scrolling differ from Mridul's month-long ban?
qa.a: Bidisha asked what need the phone was meeting and planned replacements like calling a friend, while Mridul banned everything at once, hit the school-group problem by day four and quit.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling after opening the chat on day four?
qa.a: Mridul felt discouraged, like a failure, which led to deleting the whole plan. 😔

qa.q: What could Chinmay try if he slips again?
qa.a: He could look for the trigger, plan something to do, and restart the next day without blaming himself.

grounding: Four approaches to repairing screen habits: measuring first, asking what need it meets, an all-at-once ban, and reviewing a slip without self-blame.

passage:
Long division looked like a tangle to Kalyani until she noticed it was one small cycle of four moves: split, multiply back, take away, then bring the next digit down. She practised each move alone on scrap paper, then linked two, then all four, and the tangle became a routine.

Omkar could not make sense of three-fourths. The words meant nothing until his mother cut a real roti into four equal parts and put three on his plate. He looked at the plate and said, "Oh. That's most of it."

Jahnavi had memorised a rule from a tip sheet, "flip and multiply", to split one fraction by another. Her familiar sums were all correct, and she felt proud. Then the teacher wrote a problem about sharing ribbon among friends, and Jahnavi stared at it and could not tell what to flip.

Dev kept guessing at his subtraction sums and kept getting them wrong. One evening he wrote down exactly where he got stuck: the borrowing step. The next morning he asked the teacher, "Can you show me that one step again?" and watched it slowly, twice.

qa.q: What did Omkar's mother cut into four equal parts?
qa.a: She cut a real roti into four equal parts.

qa.q: How did Omkar come to understand three-fourths, and why did that work where Jahnavi's memorised rule failed?
qa.a: Omkar saw three real pieces of a roti cut into four, so the idea made sense, while Jahnavi had memorised a rule without knowing why it works, so a new kind of problem stumped her.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she stared at the ribbon problem?
qa.a: Confused and probably worried, since her pride in her correct sums did not help her here.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try next?
qa.a: Jahnavi could cut or draw a real ribbon into equal parts to see why dividing fractions works, and ask the teacher to explain.

grounding: Four approaches to a hard maths topic: breaking it into steps, an everyday example, memorising a rule blindly, and asking a specific question.

passage:
At Nani's flat the cousins played hide and seek all afternoon, and seven-year-old Ishan was the seeker. He counted to ten with his face to the wall.

Shreya slid into the almirah, because her older cousin Meera had won there last time. Ishan checked under the bed and behind the curtain, never thought of the almirah, and Shreya won that round without knowing why it worked.

Next round Varun crouched behind the sofa and thought, "If Ishan goes left, I go right around the sofa." He waited, watching Ishan's feet, and slipped away the moment they turned left.

Little Anjali, four, stood in the centre of the floor and covered both eyes with her hands. "You can't see me!" she whispered. Ishan found her in a second, and she looked startled.

Tanvi was found behind the door in seconds. In the next round she tried the curtain and was found again. The third time she squeezed under the bed. That one held.

qa.q: Where did Shreya hide, and why?
qa.a: In the almirah, because her older cousin Meera had won there last time.

qa.q: How did Varun's way of hiding differ from Anjali's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Varun planned around Ishan's move and watched which way Ishan went, while Anjali covered her own eyes and believed she could not be seen, so Ishan found her in a second.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when Ishan found her in a second?
qa.a: Startled and puzzled, because she believed covering her eyes had made her invisible.

qa.q: How could an adult help Anjali hide better?
qa.a: An adult could play a round with her, show where a seeker looks, and suggest a spot behind something instead.

grounding: Four hide-and-seek strategies at ages four to six: copying a peer, an if-then plan, covering own eyes, and trial and error.

passage:
Baljeet printed the last three years of rounds for the company he wanted: an aptitude test, a coding round, an HR chat. Next to each he wrote how ready he felt. Coding had the widest gap, so it got the most time. Over six weeks, each day, he set aside ninety minutes on coding, forty on aptitude and thirty on speaking aloud, and kept a log of every problem he solved.

His classmate Afreen took another route for the HR round. She copied answers from the internet, scripted every line, and recited them in the mirror. In the room, the interviewer changed one question slightly, asking about a time she disagreed with a team. Afreen's voice trailed off and the rehearsed sentences would not fit.

Baljeet failed the technical round at his first company. That night he wrote down each question he missed, looked up the idea behind each, and worked the problems again. At the next company, Uma, another candidate in the waiting area, asked how the coding test went. "Easier than I feared," Baljeet said, and smiled.

qa.q: How many minutes a day did Baljeet give to aptitude practice?
qa.a: He gave forty minutes a day to aptitude.

qa.q: How did Baljeet prepare differently from Afreen, and why did his later interview go better?
qa.a: Baljeet practised regularly and, after failing, learned the idea behind each missed question, whereas Afreen memorised scripts and had no understanding to draw on when the question changed.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when her voice trailed off?
qa.a: Panic and embarrassment, since her rehearsed sentences would not fit the new question.

qa.q: What could Afreen do to prepare for the next interview?
qa.a: Afreen could practise answering in her own words from real experiences, with a friend changing the questions.

grounding: Four approaches to placement interviews: analysing the company pattern, daily time-boxed practice, memorising answers, and learning from a rejection.

passage:
At the art table on Friday, four children were making cards.

Swati folded her paper in half, drew a cake across the front, wrote her friend's name inside, and only then picked up the crayons. Each step waited its turn, and the card came together.

Tarun sat with his eyes half closed. "Nani will open it and smile," he said. Then he drew her favourite flowers, yellow marigolds, and used the orange crayon for their middles.

Tenzin's cake came out crooked. Tenzin scrunched the paper into a ball. "It's ugly," Tenzin said, and pushed away the new sheet the teacher offered. There would be no card.

Mina squeezed glitter glue over a fresh drawing, and it smeared into the picture. She took another sheet, drew in pencil first, and put the glitter only round the edge. The teacher watched her try it again and nodded.

qa.q: What did Swati draw on the front of her card?
qa.a: Swati drew a cake across the front.

qa.q: How did Tenzin's reaction to a crooked drawing differ from Mina's reaction to smeared glitter?
qa.a: Tenzin scrunched up the paper, said it was ugly and would not try again, while Mina took another sheet, drew in pencil first and put the glitter only round the edge.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when saying "It's ugly"?
qa.a: Disappointment and frustration, because the cake was not how Tenzin wanted it.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Tenzin?
qa.a: The teacher could say a crooked cake still makes a lovely card and offer to draw a new one together, without pressing.

grounding: Four approaches to making a birthday card: a step list, imagining the recipient, giving up over a flaw, and trial and error with materials.
